rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. Its line, "Without the default rate and cost terms, this angle has a visible hole," is exactly the discipline this update needs; B keeps turning gaps into copy, especially "instead of routing retailers to a bank or a BNPL provider" and "cash flow, not demand," neither of which is in the update. B has the sharper brand-side angle, but it also smuggles in enough invented scaffolding to make a founder sound over-briefed and under-proofed.
gaps_in_A: "A $12.6B private marketplace is quietly becoming a lender to 700,000 small businesses" overstates reach; the facts say Faire connects 700,000 retailers, not that all are eligible for or receiving credit.
"makes a marketplace into a credit institution" may be directionally fair, but it risks a regulatory/legal implication the update does not prove.
The trend angle admits the problem itself: "there is no supplied current news peg about B2B BNPL or platform lending." That makes it useful context, not a lead pitch.
A misses the clean supplier-side angle hiding in "brands are paid upfront while retailers pay later"; brands are not just supporting cast here.
gaps_in_B: "instead of routing retailers to a bank or a BNPL provider" and "paying brands upfront out of its own pocket" invent the funding route. The update says Faire underwrites; it does not say whose capital funds it.
"The prevailing belief in embedded finance is that platform data makes underwriting safer than a bank's" is a contrarian peg built from air. Bring evidence or cut it.
"Small shops say cash flow, not demand, is what stops them from ordering" invents the demand comparison. The update only says cash flow is the top barrier.

"won't disclose default rates" and "the refusal is itself the story" turn non-disclosure in the supplied facts into an active refusal. That is how you manufacture a fight a reporter will not thank you for.
